meta.date_display: the Thirteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

news.subhead: THE LAURELS DESK: THE LAST ENVELOPES OF THE SILVER SEASON — ALVAREZ OF HOUSTON AND CROW-ARMSTRONG OF THE NORTH SIDE ARE NAMED MOST VALUABLE ON ALL THIRTY BALLOTS APIECE, AND FOR THE FIRST TIME IN ALL THE YEARS SINCE THE PITCHERS' PRIZE WAS STRUCK, EVERY ONE OF THE SEASON'S FOUR GREAT HONORS IS UNANIMOUS
news.body:
One of them does his damage standing nearly still, the heaviest bat in the American League attached to a man who took the field just 25 times; the other plays center field like a sentry posted over the whole garden, and runs, and throws, and hits for power besides. Asked to choose between impact in its purest form and impact in all its forms, the writers declined to vote against either: the Baseball Writers' Association of America read its Most Valuable verdicts Thursday night, and Yordan Alvarez of the Astros and Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs were named first on every ballot cast in their leagues — the fourteenth unanimous choice in the American League's history and the eleventh in the National's, and only the third November, after 2023 and 2024, in which both Most Valuable prizes went without dissent.[^bbwaa-al][^bbwaa-nl] Set Wednesday's sweep by Misiorowski and Schlittler beside it and the week closes on a thing never before entered in the books: since the pitchers' prize was struck in 1956, no season had ever seen both Most Valuable awards and both Cy Youngs voted unanimously together.[^langs] The reader will recall that Wednesday's theater at Las Vegas handed its Aaron awards to precisely these two men, and that yesterday's columns called them the favorites by the wire's reckoning; the ballot has now ratified what the hint already whispered.[^castrovince-mvp]

Alvarez's season was a masterclass in the oldest arts. He led all the Majors in each of the three figures a batting line is built from — a .316 average, a .432 on-base mark, a .607 slug — just the fourth man this century to do it, after Barry Bonds in 2002, Miguel Cabrera in 2013 and Aaron Judge only last year, and he was walked intentionally 33 times, a Houston record and the second-most in American League history behind Judge's 36 of 2025.[^castrovince-mvp] The one prize that escaped him was the Triple Crown, which came apart in September: his 42 home runs and 106 driven in each finished second to Pete Alonso of the Orioles, one shy and seven shy respectively — though he is only the third man since 1970 to take the American League batting title while hitting 40 home runs, after Cabrera and Judge. He is the second man whose trade is chiefly designated hitting ever to win the award, following the door Shohei Ohtani broke down; the fourth Cuban-born Most Valuable, after José Abreu, Jose Canseco and Zoilo Versalles; and the third Astro so honored, after Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017 — with only Bagwell, like him, unanimous.[^castrovince-mvp][^langs] The trophy completes a week in which he also carried off the Aaron award, the Edgar Martínez prize and the league's Comeback honor. "I just wanted a chance," he said through an interpreter, of the boy in Cuba who dreamed smaller than this. "I wanted a chance to play professional baseball years ago. Winning the MVP, winning the World Series, none of this was in my mind. So to be here now … look at me now."[^castrovince-mvp]

Crow-Armstrong's case was the whole toolbox, and it was built from a ruin. A third of the way through the schedule the young Cub carried a .673 OPS — the lowest figure, by the statisticians' reckoning, ever carried at that depth of season by a man who finished a ten-win campaign — and from June onward he batted .305, reached at a .399 clip and slugged .663, finishing with 45 home runs, which tied for the most in the game, and 41 stolen bases: the seventh 40-40 season ever played and the first since Ohtani's of 2024 — and, counting his doubles, 30 at the least, a season's full line only Ohtani and Alfonso Soriano had ever matched.[^castrovince-mvp] He led all baseball in total bases with 357, in extra-base hits with 84 and in runs scored with 119, won his second Gold Glove, and by FanGraphs' ledger was worth 10.6 wins above a replacement man — 3.6 clear of the next name on the list, the widest daylight between first and second since Mantle over Snider in 1954.[^castrovince-mvp] At 24 years and 186 days he is the fifth-youngest unanimous Most Valuable by the Elias bureau's count; his is the tenth Most Valuable prize in the Cubs’ long books, though he is but the ninth man to carry one off, Banks having done it twice — the first Cub honored since Kris Bryant in 2016, and the first ever unanimous, this for the franchise of Banks, Sandberg and Sosa.[^langs][^bbwaa-nl] The National League's winner has now been unanimous four Novembers running, a thing that had never happened even twice in succession before 2023.[^bbwaa-nl] "I think it's just the fact that I want to be better than I was the day before," he said. "And really, that's been all that I've needed to motivate myself with for really as long as I can remember."[^castrovince-mvp]

The also-rans deserve their lines in the ledger. In the American League, Junior Caminero of the Sunshine nine totaled 267 points for second — the highest finish any Rays man has managed in the club's 29 seasons, which still wait on a first Most Valuable; their prior best was a pair of sixths from Evan Longoria and one from Yandy Díaz — with Bobby Witt Jr. of the Kansas City nine third at 188.[^bbwaa-al][^mvp-votes] In the National, the man unseated was the institution itself: Ohtani, the two-time reigning winner, his two-way labors halted and his bat dimmed by injury, stood second at 264 points, with Brice Turang of the champions third at 190.[^castrovince-mvp][^mvp-votes] And the week's four winners share one more distinction: with Misiorowski, Schlittler and Crow-Armstrong all short of their 26th birthdays at the season's close, this is only the second awards season — 1985 was the other, with Mattingly, Saberhagen and Gooden — in which three of the four great prizes went to men so young.[^langs] The silver season is now fully adjourned; the game belongs to the ink and the telephone.

news.subhead: THE EXCHANGE DESK: LAS VEGAS ADJOURNS WITH A VERDICT OF ITS OWN — THE TRADE EXPECTS SKUBAL TO LAND AMONG THE METROPOLITANS, ONE RIVAL STEWARD KNOWING NO OTHER CLUB 'EVEN IN THE CONVERSATION,' THOUGH THE SUITORS' REGISTER RUNS SIX DEEP AND THE CUBS, WANTING FIVE STARTERS, SIT OUT
news.body:
The General Managers Meetings broke camp this week, and the corridors' parting judgment concerned the winter's one great arm. The widespread expectation of the industry, as the delegates scattered homeward, is that Tarik Skubal ends the winter a Met — "I don't know who else is really even in the conversation," one National League executive said of the bidding — the Flushing club being best positioned for a man seeking a long engagement, with talk of a contract running seven years to ten.[^skubal-wire] The reader has watched this march all week: the Mets booked their audience with the left-hander for next week, as these columns recorded Wednesday, and the Blue Jays followed a day later, joining the Dodgers — his summer renters — and the Padres among the confirmed, with the Giants and the Phillies also said to have expressed interest and at least two mystery clubs besides. The arithmetic has not moved: two Cy Youngs on the mantel, and a price expected to sail past both the $325 million that Yoshinobu Yamamoto's contract marks as the guarantee record for a pitcher and the $43.33 million annual wage that Scherzer and Verlander still share.[^skubal-wire]

The curiosity of the register is the club that is not on it. The Cubs — fresh from crowning a Most Valuable, as the columns above attest — appear unlikely to enter the bidding, by the Athletic's reporting, though ESPN's man hears they want Skubal badly; and their need is no rumor, for every one of the five starters who finished the season in the Chicago rotation is now a free agent: Imanaga, Boyd, Peterson, Holmes and Gausman, the whole shelf cleared at a stroke.[^skubal-wire] A club with a unanimous laureate in center field and not one incumbent starting pitcher is a winter story this paper intends to follow with relish.

news.subhead: THE CHAMPIONS' LEDGER: MILWAUKEE MEETS THE QUESTION IT TAUGHT THE LEAGUE TO ASK — IS THE SERIES' MOST VALUABLE MAN FOR SALE? ARNOLD CALLS HIS CATCHER SPECIAL AND PROMISES NOTHING, WHILE MEGILL, KEEPER OF THE LAST SIX OUTS, COLLECTS A TESTIMONIAL FROM THE FRONT OFFICE AND AN AUDIENCE WITH METALLICA
news.body:
Matt Arnold spent his week in Las Vegas fielding the question his own house invented. William Contreras, who turns 29 on Christmas Eve, enters his final season before free agency now that his 2027 option is exercised — and the Milwaukee method with men in exactly that station is a matter of public record: Corbin Burnes sold to the Orioles on the eve of 2024's spring, Devin Williams to the Yankees the following winter, Freddy Peralta to the Mets going into 2026, each a contract-year star exchanged for prospects.[^contreras-wire] Hence the morning's question, which this paper first weighed on Tuesday: does the catcher follow the pitchers out the door, or does he follow the path of Willy Adames, the shortstop the club chose to keep for a final year and let walk for a draft pick? "I'm assuming we'll get this question a lot," the president of baseball operations allowed. "But he means a lot to our team." And further: "He's really special... You saw what he did in the postseason, how he's been able to catch 1,000 innings for three years in a row, and Silver Sluggers and All-Star appearances. I don't think we win this championship without William Contreras." The October case wants no restating — a 1.036 OPS through three rounds and the first World's Series Most Valuable honor in the franchise's books. Asked whether catchers are more like pitchers or shortstops in his calculus, Arnold gave the winter's most honest answer: "They're hard to find, that's for sure."[^contreras-wire]

The same ledger holds a second name. Trevor Megill, who turns 33 early in December, enters his last winter of arbitration off a career year — a personal-best 61 and two-thirds innings, 30 saves for a second consecutive season, and the final six outs of the World's Series — and would be coveted in his own right should Milwaukee listen.[^contreras-wire] The front office's testimony on this point is less guarded and considerably more musical: Megill, who enters to Metallica's "The Four Horsemen" at home, went to see the band at the Sphere this week while his boss was in town for the meetings, and met them besides. "He got the last six outs of the World Series, and I just went to a Metallica concert with him, so I like him," Arnold said. "I like him a lot." The Herald submits that this is the finest piece of roster analysis the meetings produced, and notes that the champions' winter — Bauers' qualifying answer due Tuesday, the catcher's telephone ringing — is only beginning.[^contreras-wire]

news.subhead: THE INK DESK: THE TOMAHAWK NINE BUY BACK THE ARM THEY MAILED AWAY EIGHT YEARS SINCE — PHILLIPS TAKES THREE YEARS AND FIVE-AND-THIRTY MILLIONS TO STEADY A BULLPEN OF MANY VACANCIES
news.body:
The week's late signature carries a homecoming in it. Evan Phillips and the Braves agreed Thursday afternoon on a contract of three years and $35 million — $11 million in each of the first two seasons and $13 million in 2029 — returning the right-hander to the organization that made him and then mailed him to Baltimore in the 2018 trade that fetched Kevin Gausman, four appearances into his Atlanta service.[^bowman] The years between tell a journeyman's romance: let go by the Orioles, claimed off the waiver wire by the Dodgers from the Rays in August of 2021, and transformed there into one of the game's steadiest late-innings men — a 1.14 earned-run average in 2022, 2.05 in 2023 — until his elbow gave out and took Tommy John surgery in May of 2025. The comeback season just closed argues the arm is whole: a 3.46 earned-run average over 31 appearances after a first half spent convalescing, a four-seamer averaging 96.9 mph — faster than he threw in either of his great Dodger years — and a strikeout rate of 31.1 percent, near his best.[^bowman]

Atlanta's need is as plain as the money. Raisel Iglesias is a free agent; Didier Fuentes, among the game's best relievers this past year, is to be stretched out as a starter in the spring, his role settled afterward; and Robert Suarez returned only in the season's final week from three months lost to a right elbow ailment. Phillips thus joins a late-innings corps being rebuilt on the fly — Suarez, Dylan Lee, the postseason revelation Ray Kerr, perhaps Iglesias again if the market returns him — and the Herald observes that the prospect Atlanta let go for nothing much in 2018 has come home at three years and $35 million — the market’s own interest, compounded over eight winters.[^bowman]

news.subhead: THE OUTFIELD MARKET: THE BROTHERLY LOVE NINE ENTER THE SUIT FOR SATO, THE YOUNGEST BAT IN A MARKET OF OLD ONES, WHILE AT SEATTLE DIPOTO ALLOWS THAT THE PLAN HE ONCE CALLED 'Z' IS NOW MERELY EXPENSIVE
news.body:
Philadelphia's outfield problem has acquired a Japanese answer. The Phillies have interest in Teruaki Sato — joining the Yankees, Mets, Dodgers and Padres in the suit for the slugger whose crossing of the Far Pacific these columns noted Tuesday — and the logic is generational arithmetic.[^zolecki] Dave Dombrowski said plainly at the meetings that his club must find an outfielder before Opening Day, and as plainly that "I'm not necessarily looking for our club to continue to get older": Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena, the market's two best outfield bats, are 32 and nearly so, with the projection houses placing each at roughly four years and $90 million to $108 million. Sato is 27 — younger than Bryson Stott, younger than Brandon Marsh — the Most Valuable of Japan's league in 2025 and its Triple Crown man in 2026, and is projected at five years and anywhere from $80 million to $115 million.[^zolecki] The caveats are real: he swings freely and strikes out plenty, bats left-handed atop a lineup already listing that way with Harper and Schwarber, and fields indifferently enough that Philadelphia would post him in right rather than at third base. And there is history to overcome — the Phillies have courted the great Japanese free agents for years and never once been chosen, Ohtani and Yamamoto, by the local accounting, having had no interest at all.[^zolecki]

On the Puget Sound, meanwhile, the unthinkable has been repriced. Jerry Dipoto, who a few winters ago called trading from his starting pitching "Plan Z," told the meetings that clubs are already calling about his rotation and that he will listen: "It'll take a lot for us to move one... But if they can make us or allow us access to a hitter we otherwise wouldn't be able to access, then we have to be open."[^kramer] The inventory explains the confidence — "We're eight deep, in my mind," he said, counting the established five of Gilbert, Kirby, Woo, Miller and Hancock, plus the rookie Kade Anderson, who debuted three weeks after the Castillo sale, the ascending Ryan Sloan and the returning Logan Evans, every man of them homegrown and all but Gilbert under club control past next season. Kirby and Hancock are reckoned the likeliest to be had.[^kramer] The object of any such commerce is the same one Wednesday's columns named when the club bade farewell to its shortstop: a bat, preferably right-handed, for a lineup that lists to port. The Herald notes that "Plan Z" has quietly become "Plan: for the right price," which is how all alphabets end in November.

desk_note: Friday the thirteenth, and the desk notes that the flannel-wearing men of the old game, who would not step on a foul line or lend a fellow their bat, somehow played this date every year without the sky falling; the Herald publishes accordingly, and without a rabbit's foot. The silver season is now complete — rookies Monday, managers Tuesday, pitchers Wednesday, and the Most Valuable pair last night, every prize of the writers' week bestowed and four of them without a single contrary ballot, as the columns above attest. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and it obliges the masthead to a small correction: the camps' reporting dates — pitchers and catchers, the first rung of winter's ladder — are still to be posted, so the paper counts instead to the first rung with a date on it, the spring exhibition slate of Friday, the 19th of February, 98 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow 131 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.[^bref] The 17th keeps its double appointment four mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — and the collective agreement has 18 mornings left to live, a figure the week's dealings at Las Vegas never once forgot. Until Saturday's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
